journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Beyond Representation: Drawing Literacy in Architectural Education, the Case of University of Belgrade, Faculty of Architecture
abstract: Abstract In the context of first and second digital paradigm shifts, this paper explores the potential of architectural drawing in contemporary architectural education. Through examining historical sources, defining methods for their analytical reading and conducting a case study, this paper identifies that architectural drawing is both an analytical and a critical tool for conceptual exploration. The study focuses on architectural education within the design studio course as the primary domain where the research potential of drawing is most evident. Through the critical analysis of selected student projects nominated for the RIBA President's Medals Student Awards (2011–2024) from the University of Belgrade, Faculty of Architecture, the research reveals the evolving role of drawing as a medium for architectural expression, experimentation and critique. It underscores the ambivalence of architectural drawing as both a means of precise technical representation and a speculative tool for conceptual inquiry. journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Building Pathways in Architectural Education: Educating the Un‐Architect
abstract: Abstract Architectural education faces mounting pressure to rethink its pedagogies in response to technological, environmental and social change. Inspired by Allan Kaprow's concept of the ‘un‐artist’ (1971), this article introduces the un‐architect as a transdisciplinary, reflexive practitioner who resists institutional hierarchy, values process over product and treats architecture as civic practice. Drawing on historical and contemporary shifts in pedagogy, and through theoretical analysis and selected case studies, the article argues that architectural education must move beyond specialisation and commodified knowledge towards integrative, ethically grounded learning centred on community engagement, ecological responsibility and participatory design. It calls for a redefinition of architectural education as a space of critical inquiry and shared authorship—where learning is co‐creation rather than instruction—and positions the un‐architect as a position for cultivating adaptability, creativity and social consciousness indispensable for navigating the complexities of 21st‐century practice.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Teaching Visual Communication Design Histories Through Critical Annotation and Public Archiving: A Story in Five Artefacts
abstract: Abstract This pedagogical case study explores how participatory pedagogy might transform design history education. The study draws on 8 years of working with design history students to recuperatively document visual communication design history artefacts and practitioners. For 3 years, this experience focused on collaborating with students to contribute 1000+ entries directly to the People's Graphic Design Archive (PGDA), an online, crowd‐sourced archive of diverse design histories. Approaching self‐reflexive teaching praxis as action research, this article synthesises the work of writing personalised weekly responses to +/− 5580 annotated design artefacts. The qualitative, mixed methods approach combines auto‐ethnographic writing, document analysis and critically informed historical contextualisation. After interrogating what design history means and situating crowd‐sourced archival work within a disciplinary framework, the author presents five representative examples of designed artefacts that typify students' contributions to the PGDA. journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Emotional Expression and Self‐Care: A Participatory Design Approach to Art Education with Left‐Behind Children in Rural China
abstract: Abstract This study explores the emotional support of ‘left‐behind children’ in rural China by integrating Participatory Design (PD) methods into art education to foster emotional expression and self‐care. Drawing on an eight‐year longitudinal case study involving questionnaires ( n = 189 children), multiple workshops, semi‐structured interviews and the development of pedagogical tools, this paper focuses on two PD practices: ‘A Cup of Story Time’ and ‘My Parents in My Mind’ and one collaborative art education toolkit. Findings indicate that PD‐based teaching can disrupt the traditional technique‐oriented paradigm of rural art education, transforming the classroom into a space for emotional exchange between children and their absent parents. Children were encouraged to express love in their creations, cultivating a sense of self‐care and peer support. Moreover, the art classroom functioned as a trust‐building environment that strengthened children's subjectivity and emotional identity. As a low‐cost, participatory, and emotionally restorative intervention, this model reshapes relational dynamics in rural education, positioning children as collaborators and active agents in teaching

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Creativity in Crisis or Crisis in Creativity? A Problem‐Finding Study of Artist‐Teachers in Indian Schools
abstract: Abstract Art education plays a vital role in nurturing creativity, confidence and curiosity among students, yet the lived realities of art educators remain underexplored. This study seeks to identify and analyse the key challenges faced by artist‐teachers in Indian schools, with a focus on how institutional, systemic and cultural factors shape their professional and personal experiences. Sixteen artist‐teachers, eight from government schools and eight from private schools, participated in semi‐structured interviews. The data were examined through thematic analysis to uncover recurring patterns and underlying issues. The analysis reveals that both government and private school art teachers encounter persistent structural and professional barriers. Government school teachers struggle with inadequate resources, unsuitable classroom environments and limited administrative support. Private school teachers, though better resourced, report marginal funding for art programmes and the relegation of art to a decorative or auxiliary function within the school system. journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Patience Stones: Material Encounters for Slow Currents of Pedagogy
abstract: Abstract This article moves across sites in Canada and Japan with the practice of making Patience Stones (Sang‐e Saboor), a biodegradable, dough‐based artistic and pedagogical object that invites artist–teachers and artist–learners into with‐nessing and slow becoming. Drawing through a/r/tography, material encounter and artist–teacher practice, the inquiry approaches pedagogy as an emergent, layered and relational field shaped through wandering, touching, waiting and being‐with. Working with elementary and university students, the making of soft, air‐dry stones becomes a pedagogical companion for thinking through patience, plurality and reciprocal forms of relations. Interweaving and contextualising fragments of narratives, visual documentations, poetic propositions and theory, the article (re)visits and (re)orients inherited understandings of patience in Persian and Japanese contexts, troubling the glorification of endless endurance often expected within education and institutions. Against accelerated cultures of productivity, extraction and educational legibility, the article proposes the ‘slow currents of pedagogy’ as practices of softness, companionship, pliability and shared b

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Learning Challenges in Design Education and Barriers to Gamification Adoption
abstract: Abstract While gamification holds potential to address learning challenges in tertiary design education, research has focused mainly on student performance, with less attention to educators' role in implementation. This study addresses this gap by identifying learner‐level challenges and exploring educators' perceptions of gamification and barriers to adoption. A three‐phase design was employed. Phase 1 systematically reviewed 154 publications spanning 2002–2025 and classified reported challenges using a Bloom‐informed cognitive, affective and psychomotor framework. Phase 2 synthesised literature to develop challenge–mechanism alignments between these challenges and relevant gamification elements and mechanisms. Phase 3 involved semi‐structured interviews with ten design educators from seven higher education institutions in China. Affective and cognitive challenges were most prominent in the reviewed literature, whereas psychomotor challenges were comparatively underrepresented. journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Legitimate Incompletion: Artistic Formation and the Temporal Logic of Studio Art Education
abstract: Abstract Studio art degrees routinely certify artistic competence within bounded periods of academic study, despite longstanding associations between mastery and extended training. This article examines how this tension became pedagogically and institutionally plausible through a twentieth‐century redefinition of evaluative criteria in studio practice. Drawing on scholarship in studio pedagogy, professional formation and tacit knowledge, the article traces how postwar modernism reframed competence in terms of sustained inquiry, reflective positioning and the coherence of exploratory work. It argues that this revaluation enabled academic programmes to recognise readiness for artistic participation prior to the consolidation of technical expertise. The concept of legitimate incompletion is introduced to describe this condition, in which incomplete formation is treated as professionally sufficient within degree structures. By examining critique‐centred assessment, capstone review practices and accreditation frameworks, the article shows how academic institutions stabilise a temporal ordering in which recognition precedes experiential depth. journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: A Visual Brainstorming Technique in Character Design: Braindrawing
abstract: Abstract Character design is a complex design process that requires originality, narrative depth and visual consistency all at once. However, students often approach the idea‐generation process using intuitive and unsystematic methods. This study aims to examine the pedagogical potential of the braindrawing technique in graphic design education. The research was designed as a practice‐based qualitative case study conducted in a classroom setting. A total of 69 students participated in the study, and the open‐ended comments of 47 students were analysed using thematic analysis. Additionally, student work and observations made throughout the process were included in the dataset. The findings indicate that the braindrawing technique increases students' idea diversity, helps them overcome creative blocks and supports collaborative interaction. It was observed that the process contributed to students developing more original and narratively strong character designs. By focusing on the use of the braindrawing technique in the context of character design and illustration education, this study contributes to the literature on design education.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: DARE: A Live Art Methodology that Embraces Disruption Towards a Pedagogy of Agonism
abstract: Abstract This paper presents a new live art methodology for secondary education art classrooms, designed and tested through action research. This research investigated how pedagogical elements of live art, an embodied art practice not yet included in the secondary art curriculum, contribute to young people's development. It emerged in the context of the globalised crisis in education that instrumentalises and marginalises arts subjects. In contrast, I developed an approach that frames art as a process‐based pedagogy that uses disruptions as productive tensions, inspired by agonism (a political concept that emerged in the 1960s). I present DARE (Disruptive, Artistic, Reflexive, Exploration), a methodology that uses disruption and critical reflexivity identified as elements of live art that can transform education. DARE builds on a radical constructivist educational theory that embraces discomfort as dialogic knowledge production. Through examples of students' actions, I examine how tensions inherent in the formation of identity in adolescents become moments of learning through performance, often unravelling on the edge of chaos. journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Making Art or Studying Art? Routes to Ecological Thinking in the Secondary School Classroom
abstract: Abstract Art education scholarship has increasingly turned towards relational, ecological ways of thinking about the subject. This article asks whether that turn is reflected in how Art education is experienced and justified in the classroom. Drawing on interviews with students and an Art teacher in a rural state secondary school in England, it finds that Art education was most frequently justified through transferable skills. Using two contrasting examples of classroom practice, the article identifies two distinct routes by which Art education might cultivate ecological thinking: one through experimental making, whose effects are framed ontologically; the other through studying ecologically engaged contemporary art. Evidence of students initially unable to read an installation addressing biodiversity loss illustrates how the second route depends on a capacity the article terms art literacy—the ability to understand how a work relates to existing art concepts, precedents and conventions, without which much ecologically engaged contemporary art remains illegible and alienating to students. The article argues that developing art literacy offers a more modest yet defensible and legibl

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: The Classroom as a Work of Art
abstract: Abstract This article is the product of a project that stems from an educational environment, challenges it, and aims to transcend its boundaries. Within the project, the ordinary flow of a classroom was intervened with through play, and ways to reunite students – who are often perceived as ‘surpluses’ within the current education system – were explored. The theoretical foundation of the study is based on Félix Guattari's question: ‘How do you bring a classroom to life as if it were a work of art?’ This study argues that when a teacher is not limited to a studio practice as an artist but approaches the space where art occurs through a mental transformation, all components of the classroom carry the potential to transform into a work of art. While traditional educational approaches generally prioritise the final product and outcomes, this study emphasises that a process‐oriented curriculum allows more room for experimentation for both the teacher and the student. This project, where art and education are intertwined, enables the development of a more conceptual and contemporary teacher/artist practice, aiming to resonate both with the students directly involved in the process and wi

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Seeing AI in the Art & Design Classroom: Exploring the Material Conditions for Critical Visual Literacy
abstract: Abstract Drawing on an ongoing research project that has brought together teachers and artists as co‐researchers, this paper considers the implications of image‐based Generative AI for teaching and learning in the UK art and design classroom. We explore some of the challenges posed by AI to art and design education in 2026, following a period in which the subject has been marginalised in favour of STEM subjects. We are interested in what art and design brings to this discussion, particularly in relation to images produced by Generative AI, and in establishing correspondence with earlier pedagogical responses to visual culture and new media. We are interested in placing artistic and critical approaches at the centre of this discussion and adopting a hands‐on approach that is ‘unplugged’ from digital systems. John Berger's 1972 Ways of Seeing is our key influence, reminding us of the continued importance of issues concerning the reproduction of bias and forms of privilege through visual culture, and the changing relation between seeing and knowledge production. journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Enhancing Creative Confidence in Design Students Through Topology‐Preserving AI Scaffolding
abstract: Abstract Early‐stage design students frequently experience representational friction during conceptual ideation, where limited sketch fluency constrains the externalisation of spatial concepts and weakens creative confidence. This study examines whether a topology‐preserving generative AI framework can function as a pedagogical cognitive scaffold to reduce these barriers without displacing student authorship. We implemented a zero‐shot, structure‐guided AI system (based on ControlNet) that converts hand‐drawn sketches into structurally mediated visual scaffolds while preserving original geometric topology. In a controlled experiment (), this AI‐assisted workflow was compared with static moodboard‐based ideation. To isolate design logic from surface rendering advantages, blind experts evaluated only final pure line‐art outcomes. Results indicated that the AI‐assisted group was associated with higher overall design quality ( d = 0.88), with improvements concentrated in structural coherence, functionality, and completeness rather than aesthetic quality. title: Third‐Site Ecologies in Art Education: Artist‐Teacher Perspectives on Environmental Awareness in Turkey
abstract: Abstract This study examines how ecological awareness is fostered through art education in Turkey from the perspective of artist‐teachers who teach in higher education and integrate their artistic and teaching practices. Designed as a qualitative study, data were collected via semi‐structured interviews with artist‐teachers working in various regions of Turkey. Participants were selected using purposive sampling based on their delivery of ecology‐focused lessons and active involvement in ecological art practices. The findings indicate that, whilst ecological art serves as a pedagogical tool supporting environmental awareness, it also contributes to the formation of a relational pedagogical space that emerges at the intersection of art production and teaching practice. In this field, ecological awareness is cultivated through experiential, process‐oriented, and critical forms of learning. The fact that artist‐teachers pursue their production and teaching processes in tandem repositions teaching as an extension of artistic practice and transforms learning environments into multilayered structures. The study conceptualises this intersection as a ‘third‐site’ pedagogical field and argu

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Re‐Walking Betweenness: Augmented Reality as a Pedagogy of Geo‐Historical Justice
abstract: Abstract This article proposes a pedagogical approach that mobilises AR as an apparatus within artistic practice, examining how augmented reality and hauntological walking generate embodied encounters that reconfigure spatial justice through decolonial and relational walking practices. As a settler educator and researcher, I navigate the ‘betweenness’ of Nanjing W. Road in Taiwan, the flashpoint of the 228 Incident, and Pacific Spirit Regional Park in Vancouver, through an AR approach. This inquiry demonstrates how re‐walking geo‐historical routes through AR reveals silenced histories, enabling a reflexive, justice‐oriented engagement with haunting, memory and spatial realities. Drawing on Derrida's (2006) concept of hauntology and Springgay & Truman's (2018) walking methodology, this study frames augmented reality (AR) walking as a pedagogical apparatus. Situated within an arts‐based inquiry approach (Leavy 2018), the study mobilises AR overlays of historical artefacts and narratives onto physical landscapes, transforming walking into a multi‐layered and relational learning practice. The study adopts diffractive analysis (Murris & Bozalek 2019) to examine the relations and phenome

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Meeting the New (Old) Ecological Challenges for Art Education
abstract: Abstract The discussion examines the emerging ecological critique of art education, which frames artistic production, especially in the plastic arts, as environmentally unsustainable due to its reliance on non‐essential material consumption. I argue that this critique, while contemporary in form, echoes long‐standing philosophical concerns, beginning with Plato's dismissal of art as wasteful and socially detrimental. The paper challenges the conclusion that art education is ecologically unjustifiable by drawing on the aesthetics of Kant and Dewey. Both philosophers present aesthetic experience as a mode of disinterested and perceptually rich engagement with the world. On this basis, I propose that art education cultivates non‐instrumental attention and anti‐consumerist dispositions, aligning it with ecological aims rather than opposing them. The paper concludes by outlining implications for environmentally attuned art education practices.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Collaborative occasions of imagination: A philosophical pedagogical approach to arts education in the classroom
abstract: Abstract The aim of this paper is to outline the activities of an innovative, interdisciplinary public engagement programme delivered by a team from education, art and philosophy disciplines at a Scottish university. The programme began in 2018 and has continually evolved since then in response to its work with schools. The activities are inspired by a radio play written by Walter Benjamin (1892–1940) and combine art education and philosophical approaches in the primary classroom to support young children to engage with issues that affect their everyday lives as well as develop their understanding of both subjects. The author critically reflects on this in relation to Biesta's theory of a world‐centred education and considers a new model for art education with implications for further development.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Fostering Students' Creative Collaboration Through Multimodal Design Within Virtual Worlds
abstract: Abstract As virtual worlds (VWs) continue to evolve, their potential to transform creative and collaborative learning in art and design education is increasingly evident. Yet, their integration into higher education curricula through multimodal design remains underexplored. This study responds to that gap by embedding VW technologies into an undergraduate Design Fundamentals course, reimagined through a design thinking framework and examined using a social semiotic approach. Conducted over 8 weeks, the course invited 15 university art and design students who had completed foundational coursework to create immersive, group‐based projects within virtual environments. Employing an action research approach, the study involved iterative cycles of planning, implementation and multimodal analysis to investigate how students engaged with VW affordances to develop collaborative design practices. Findings revealed that students recontextualised cultural references, negotiated visual languages, co‐constructed multimodal narratives and cultivated creative agency through iterative experimentation, while building their creative confidence for advanced design learning. journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: The glitch as insight: Digital neocolonialism, parody and critical AI literacy in the Indonesian digital media studio
abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into creative industries has intensified a ‘crisis of representation’, where the speed of production often masks deep‐seated cultural biases. This study investigates a studio‐based pedagogical intervention in a Cultural Studies class for third‐semester Indonesian digital media students, designed to support a transition from functional AI use to critical AI literacy (CAIL). Drawing on digital neocolonialism, semiotics, critical media literacy and production‐based pedagogy, the study operationalises ‘AI failure’ or the glitch, not as a technical error to be corrected, but as a productive site for learning. Through a design‐based research intervention, students generated culturally specific AI images, analysed misrepresentations through Barthes and Hall, and transformed their critiques into parody videos. The findings show that parody‐based making helped students move from passive acceptance or surface error‐spotting towards oppositional decoding and culturally grounded critique. journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Bang (방) Social Gatherings as Collaborative Inquiry Space: Rethinking Research through Informal Social Gatherings in Art Education
abstract: Abstract This article explores the concept of ‘ bang (방)’, a Korean term denoting a social gathering space, as an innovative framework for a research and professional development space in art education. Since May 2022, six authors, all Korean immigrant art education researchers, have engaged in weekly virtual ‘ Zoombang ’ sessions to share personal experiences, pedagogical issues and socio‐political topics in an unstructured format. Through these informal gatherings, we cultivated a vibrant community that values empathy and collaboration, ultimately reshaping our identities as researchers and educators. Our findings highlight the significance of social gatherings as a powerful means of knowledge sharing and community building, emphasising the collective growth and empowerment that emerges from such spaces. This paper argues that informal social gatherings like bang (방) can serve as vital sites for critical discourse and professional development in art education research and practices.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Fostering Creative Thinking and Ingenuity in Design Education: Curriculum Practices in the Beijing Institute of Fashion Technology MFA Illustration Programme
abstract: Abstract Against the backdrop of rapid changes in technology and the media environment, design education has increasingly emphasized creativity; however, creativity alone is no longer sufficient to meet the demands of contemporary design practice for the ability to solve complex problems. This paper distinguishes between the concepts of creativity and ingenuity: creativity focuses on generating novel and appropriate ideas, while ingenuity emphasizes the ability to construct viable solutions under constraints, with incomplete information, and in complex situations. Based on this dual perspective, this paper examines the curriculum of the Beijing Institute of Fashion Technology MFA Illustration program. The curriculum comprises three interrelated domains: cultural cognition, material practice, and technological intervention. journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Printmaking as a Propaedeutic Space in Contemporary Art Education
abstract: Abstract This article examines the relevance and formative value of printmaking within contemporary higher art education. Through a historical and conceptual review, it analyses the shift of printmaking from industrial and reproductive functions toward a space of artistic exploration, material enquiry and pedagogical reflection. The study argues that printmaking serves as a propaedeutic discipline that helps students understand the relationships among idea, material, time and process in artistic creation. Drawing on contributions from William M. Ivins Jr., Walter Benjamin, John Dewey, Elliot W. Eisner, Stanley William Hayter, María del Mar Bernal and Etienne Wenger, as well as experiences at the University of the West of England, the Universitat Politècnica de València and the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, the article highlights the print studio as a setting for exploratory and project‐based learning. In the digital era, it remains a space where technical, conceptual and ethical development converge.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Unseen Voices: Exam‐Oriented Art Education in China and Its Impact on Artistic Subjectivity
abstract: Abstract This study examines an exam‐oriented art education in China, highlighting how art‐training centres enforce standardised evaluation criteria and prioritise technical mastery over creative freedom. I draw from personal experience to analyse how such systems shape art examinees' artistic development and marginalise their voices, providing a missing insider perspective through autoethnography. Guided by Foucault's power theory, this research critiques the dominance of standardised assessments in art education and rethinks the rationalisation of operating exams through the lens of artistic subjectivity. At the same time, this research advocates culturally sensitive and inclusive curricula that support students transitioning from exam‐oriented systems into global educational contexts.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Exploring Complex Historical Figures through a Modified Critical Making Framework
abstract: Abstract This paper examines ‘critical making’ as a framework for exploring complex problems and topics. Critical making combines an iterative process of making with research, reflection and analysis. The authors present a modified critical making process that builds on the reflexive material engagement introduced by the originator of critical making, Matt Ratto and the more structured approach formulated by Garnet Hertz. To illustrate its application, we present a case study applying this adapted critical making model to investigate the contributions of two early female architects, Isabel Roberts and Marion Mahony Griffin. This case study employs a modified five‐phase approach that consists of research, ideation, further research, prototyping and reflection. We conclude that critical making fosters critical thinking and enables engagement with complex topics that are challenging to address with traditional research methods. Beyond a theoretical concept, practical opportunities are discussed for incorporating critical making into educational settings and scholarship.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: A Review of the Evolution of Research on the Size of Children's Drawings in Relation to Their Expressed Emotion About the Depicted Topic: 1988–2023
abstract: Abstract This narrative review examines the relationship between the size of children's drawings and their expressed emotions about the depicted subjects, focusing on research conducted between 1988 and 2023. The studies are presented chronologically to demonstrate how researchers have progressively addressed methodological challenges identified in earlier work. Some of them reached statistically significant results that connected drawing size with expressed emotion, while others did not. They attributed these results mainly to the mechanism of attraction of positive emotions that lead to the enlargement of the drawn objects or repulsion of negative emotions with the opposite effect and secondarily to pictorial conventions. These conflicting results across studies are presented, and interpretations and implications for art education are proposed. The review highlights that professionals such as art educators should take the size parameter into account with particular care, taking into consideration some additional factors such as the expression of emotions by the children themselves.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Studio Pedagogy in Transition: Lecturers' Reflections on Creative Arts Education in a Post‐COVID World
abstract: Abstract This paper presents findings from interviews with creative arts academics examining how the COVID‐19 disruption reshaped studio‐based teaching practices and informed future pedagogical thinking. Participants described the disruption as a period that compelled rapid adaptation and created opportunities to experiment, review and reflect on their teaching practices. Staff are committed to learning from this time. Lecturers expressed a strong preference for in‐person teaching, with the purposeful integration of online and digital pedagogies seen as key to expanding studio teaching. Our results suggest increased interest in the potential benefits of a blended approach. Results also revealed that the COVID‐19 disruption triggered deeper, systemic shifts in student behaviour and in teaching mindsets, changes they understood as extending beyond short‐term crisis responses and signalling more fundamental change. These findings reflect educator accounts, and we therefore interpret claims about student engagement as staff perceptions that warrant triangulation in future research.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Evaluations of Architectural Students Performance in Design Studio Related With Their Personal Type: A View From Enneagram
abstract: Abstract The Enneagram, which identifies nine personality types, is widely used in psychology, communication and management. Applying it to architectural education could be beneficial, as each personality type presents distinct strengths and challenges in academic settings. Architectural design studios emphasise creative problem‐solving, with students approaching tasks differently based on their cultural background, academic knowledge and personality. This study investigated the relationship between Enneagram personality types and the performance of architectural students in a 14‐week design studio. Using the RHETI method developed by Riso and Hudson, each student's personality type was identified and verified through interviews. The study examined students' semester performance and final design studio presentations. Results suggest that personality type can have a significant impact on overall performance in design studios. Understanding their personality type can help students manage their design projects more effectively. Additionally, instructors can use this insight to better understand student motivations and tailor their teaching strategies to support diverse learning styles

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Artists in Nursery Schools: Enabling Free Play and Self‐Expression Through the Arts
abstract: Abstract The purpose of this research was to analyse the presence of artists in nursery schools by means of two proposals to promote free play and self‐expression for children between one and 3 years‐old and their families. Researchers compiled evidence from the perspective of three atelieristas and other participating adults, through interviews and group discussions, graphic documentation and observation notes. The results shed light on the definition of the preliminary approach and the goals set by the artists in order to enable free play and self‐expression; the identification and description of their changing roles; and delved further into the attitudes and skills to carry out these experiences. The main conclusions highlight their significant artistic mediation work when they encourage self‐expression, experimenting and free play for children and their families, and the importance of the artists' sensitive attitude and active listening. They contribute to the ongoing training of these professionals, the teachers and even families, by providing keys for improvement.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Design Instructors in Focus: Unveiling the Role of Guest Speakers in Architectural Education
abstract: Abstract This study explores the role of guest speakers in architectural education, focusing on instructors' experiences with this emerging practice. While most research in higher education examines students' perspectives, little attention has been given to how instructors engage with and perceive guest speakers' events. To address the gap in the literature, this study investigates the experiences of design instructors who frequently invite guest speakers, using semi‐structured interviews. A bottom‐up approach was then applied to the analysis, allowing themes to emerge inductively from the data. This study examines how instructors navigate opportunities and challenges arising from incorporating guest speakers into their courses on their teaching and learning practices. Insights from instructors indicate that the guests affect their (1) personal growth: through motivation, inspiration, and creativity, (2) pedagogical practices: knowledge through practice, and interdisciplinary collaboration, and (3) delivery methods of knowledge: diverse presentation styles. journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Determining Visual Art Curriculum Topics Through Student Negotiation: A Case Study in a Presidential School
abstract: Abstract The study focuses on determining negotiated curriculum topics for grades 5 (11‐year‐old students) and 6 (12‐year‐old students) for Presidential and Specialised Schools in Uzbekistan. Traditionally, the visual art curriculum has been decided and provided by authorities with no influence from students. Accordingly, this study explores how student perspectives can be systematically incorporated into an existing collaboratively developed visual arts curriculum in a Presidential school, with the aim of identifying specific content areas that may inform future curriculum refinement. Negotiating a curriculum was understudied in the educational context of Uzbekistan. This is a qualitative study with quantitative components and examines how a visual art curriculum could be shaped through negotiation with students. The questions were: (1) How many topics does the curriculum include if created in collaboration with students? (2) What topics will most students accept after negotiations to add to the curriculum? (3) How many new topics will appear compared to the regular curriculum? Results demonstrated that students successfully developed a negotiated curriculum, identifying relevant

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Doing Autoethnography, Teaching Autoethnography as a White Woman Architect‐Educator‐Researcher in South Africa
abstract: Abstract This autoethnographic study lies at the intersection of architectural, teaching and research practice through the lens of an architect‐teacher‐researcher working in post‐Apartheid South Africa. The research traces a shift from unconscious design practice to a more conscious, critical and careful practice through practice‐based design research methods of drawing, photography and writing. Each method reveals a different tacit knowledge of design practice, including institutional influence and the role of past lived spatial experience. In doing so a feminist critical spatial practice was sought. Through doing and teaching autoethnography, the architect‐teacher‐researcher critically situated the self within a multicultural postcolonial educational context. Thus, the politics of whiteness was unpacked and pedagogical strategies of engaged listening, silence, collaborative, participatory and student‐centred learning were explored. Autoethnography validated diverse worldviews and ways of seeing and being in the design studio thus contributing to the researcher's and students' practice becoming more conscious, critical and careful within the post‐Apartheid architectural practice a

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Embodied Narrations: Video Narrative Inquiry for Meaning‐Making of Learning Contexts
abstract: Abstract This text begins with the initial question of how we can narrate in a situated and meaningful way about the processes of teaching and learning, not to repeat what we imagine that we should say and already know, but to be truthful with respect to the issues that affect us and matter to us. For this purpose, by moving towards the ways of doing of the visual and performing arts, we explore the possibilities offered by video narration to signify these teaching and learning experiences, giving space and presence to our bodies, which are oriented towards different attachments, thoughts and other elements that are important to us. In the present case study based on the embodied narrations collected from 2021 to 2023 in the context of the Master's degree programme in Teacher Training in Art Education at the University of the Basque Country (EHU), we reflect on the use and contribution of video narration to relate these teaching and learning processes in a situated, relational and meaningful way.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Metaphors as Critical Pedagogy: Guiding Creative Thinking in Novice Design and Non‐Design Foundation Year University Students in the United Arab Emirates
abstract: Abstract This article evaluates the use of metaphors as a technique for prompting creative thinking in design education, specifically within the context of a university pre‐entry foundation course, ‘Introduction to Design’ in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Both the student transition to higher education and global standardization practices in higher education present challenges when fostering creative thinking. With metaphorical thinking exercises and a mind‐wandering method, students are encouraged to pursue creative connections with disparate topics, moving beyond literalism to more conceptual and imaginative ideas. The study's methodological framework is grounded in an art‐based action research approach, which positions the lecturer as a reflective practitioner and encourages a participatory role from students. Our critical reflection suggests that while students generally respond positively to a metaphorical teaching technique, a portion struggle with the transition from rote or standardized learning to creative ideation. Despite these challenges, the metaphor technique along with mind wandering present distinct pedagogical value, particularly in promoting creative thinking pr

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: ‘I'm Just Not Artistic’—An Exploration of Initial Teacher Education Trainees' Confidence in Their Art Ability and their Perceptions of Teaching the Primary Art and Design Curriculum
abstract: Abstract This study explores the ongoing debate surrounding the degradation of art and design in primary education and the perceptions of trainee teachers preparing to teach the subject. It provides a starting point for further research into the role of initial teacher education (ITE) in reframing trainee teachers' conceptions of the nature and importance of the art and design curriculum. This qualitative study interviewed six trainee teachers at the beginning of their first year of teacher education to ascertain their experiences of art to date and explore themes around artistic confidence and preparedness for teaching primary art. The data indicate a surprising trend where trainee teachers have little confidence in their own artistic abilities yet consider themselves effective future art teachers. The study identifies a number of common misconceptions around the nature of primary art as a subject that is fun, low‐stakes and expendable as well as highlighting key tensions about trainees' perception of artistic skill as pre‐ordained rather than learned.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Integrating Arts Into Nature Education for Sustainable Rural Development
abstract: Abstract Rural environments offer abundant ecological and cultural resources that support the development of nature education, but practical challenges persist in fully utilising these local resources. Building on this context, the study examines an arts‐integrated nature education curriculum implemented in Jianlou Village, Hunan Province, to explore how artistic practices can enrich rural nature‐based learning. Using qualitative analysis, 49 documents—including teaching plans, student artworks, field observation notes and reflective journals—were coded and analysed using NVivo. Research indicates that art can be integrated into three key domains: site preparation, instructional approaches and curriculum materials. This integration deepens learners' engagement with the rural environment, enhances the quality of nature education activities and advances local educational development. The framework provides theoretical insights and practical guidance for curriculum innovation, teacher professional development and the advancement of art‐integrated nature education in rural communities.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Synergising Computational and Design Thinking in Design Education: A Dual‐Process Framework to Enhancing Creativity and Appropriateness
abstract: Abstract This study addressed the critical challenge of integrating computational thinking (CT) and design thinking (DT) in design education, a necessity further amplified by the rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance both creativity and appropriateness in design outcomes. Grounded in cognitive theory, a novel dual‐process framework is proposed and validated, synergising CT's algorithmic rigour with DT's iterative empathy within a structured two‐dimensional ontology space. In an experiment on fashion pattern design, AI style transfer extended human‐originated concepts. Using a mixed‐methods approach—combining eye‐tracking, subjective ratings and expert evaluation—results demonstrate that CT‐extended designs significantly outperformed human‐originated counterparts in creativity (originality, usefulness) and appropriateness (thematic relevance, aesthetic satisfaction). The findings support the framework's efficacy in expanding the solution space while ensuring contextual coherence, balancing divergent and convergent processes. Theoretically, it contributes a validated dual‐process model; methodologically, a replicable multimodal protocol; and practi

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Ctrl + Alt + Studio: Exploring Educational Capital and Social Dynamics in Virtual Studios
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates how moving the architectural design studio from its conventional physical setting to an online multi‐user virtual environment (MUVE) affects students' social dynamics. Building on Pierre Bourdieu's concepts of educational capital, habitus and field alongside Jozef Bochenski's theories of authority, the authors employed a quasi‐experimental approach with 15 architecture students who completed design tasks in a MUVE while experiencing different forms of tutor‐imparted educational capital—specifically written critiques and letter grades. Data collection through linkography, observations and retrospective interviews facilitated analysis of how authority manifests among students in this remediated environment. The findings reveal that MUVEs transform the studio's ‘field’, requiring students to adapt their established habitus while fostering new forms of educational capital tied to technical competence. Letter grades undergo devaluation in virtual environments, while written critiques gain prominence as indicators of epistemic skill. Praised students gained authority among peers and led design conversations with critical verbalisations (CVs), while in gra

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: The Mokuhanga Technique Today: An Exploration of Traditional Japanese Art in the Artistic and Educational Context
abstract: Abstract In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the Mokuhanga technique, a traditional Japanese printmaking method, and its contemporary evolution. This article explores the history of this discipline, its technical uniqueness, and its resurgence in the current context, with particular attention to its development in Spain. The main research questions are: How has Mokuhanga evolved in the Spanish context? And what impact could its integration into higher education have on students' creative development? Through a qualitative approach combining interviews with specialised artists, analysis of representative works, and a review of the current artistic landscape, this study investigates the creative and technical processes that define Mokuhanga 's distinctiveness. Furthermore, the impact of integrating Mokuhanga into higher education is analysed, highlighting its cultural relevance and its contribution to enriching the academic environment. The findings indicate that Mokuhanga revitalises contemporary printmaking as an interdisciplinary medium for artistic experimentation and that its inclusion in educational settings fosters interdisciplinary experimentation and the cr

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Extending Computer Graphics Education Through Reverse Engineering: Further Enhancements in Visual Communication and Creativity
abstract: Abstract This paper proposes a novel approach to enhancing visual communication skills and creativity in computer graphics (CG) education. The research focuses on topics related to artistic expression and visual communication within CG education and does not cover other subjects in this field, including technical aspects, such as programming skills, algorithm development, rendering techniques and simulation technologies. Using reverse engineering methodologies, we developed the ‘philosophical observation decomposition table’ and the ‘concept decomposition chart’, based on which we created an educational programme for analysing the relationships between language and visual and artistic elements. The results of this study, which was conducted with 240 first‐year students studying CG at a vocational school, include confirmed improvements in students' insight and observation, expression and comprehension skills, as well as an increased interest in human–AI collaboration. This study fills a crucial gap in CG education in the AI era and contributes to innovation in the field's curricula.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Reframing Pedagogical Practices Through the UTBO ‐ CLIL Framework in Art and Design Higher Education
abstract: Abstract This study investigates how university instructors enact CLIL (Content and Language Integrated Learning) pedagogy within art and design courses, emphasising the interaction between creative practice and linguistic scaffolding. Drawing on the University Teaching Behaviour Observation for CLIL (UTBO‐CLIL) framework, data were collected from virtual classroom observations, semi‐structured interviews and 6 weeks of reflective journals from instructors and students. The analysis identified three dominant behaviour patterns: directive, facilitative and managerial, revealing tensions between fostering creativity and maintaining linguistic precision. While directive instruction predominated during complex design tasks, instructors demonstrated emerging awareness of multimodal and constructivist strategies to enhance learner autonomy. The findings extend the UTBO‐CLIL framework to creative disciplines and contribute to the theoretical understanding of multimodal pedagogy in bilingual higher education.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Rethinking Methodology Matters in Art and Design Education Research Through the White Cube

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Effect of Artistic Activities on Adolescents' Creative Thinking: The Mediating Role of Creative Engagement
abstract: Abstract This study constructed a theoretical framework to analyse the relationship between artistic activities and creative thinking, examining both their external manifestations and underlying mechanisms. Utilising data from 9074 middle school students in Hong Kong and Macao, sourced from the 2022 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA 2022), the study employed structural equation modelling (SEM) to empirically investigate these relationships. Results indicate that artistic activities enhance adolescents' creative thinking through the mediating role of creative engagement, which involves active participation in knowledge creation, creative expression and creative problem‐solving. The study confirms that knowledge creation, creative expression and creative problem‐solving serve as core pathways through which creative engagement fosters creative thinking. Collective artistic activities, in particular, exhibit a pronounced effect on promoting creative thinking. Furthermore, gender differences observed from these pathways suggest potential biases embedded in socio‐cultural and educational environments. These findings underscore the need to improve more diverse, inclusiv

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: From Theatre to XR: Shaping Immersive Storytelling Design Education through Artistic and Analogue Insights
abstract: Abstract In an increasingly technology‐driven world, this study examined how communication design students can critically and creatively master advanced digital tools to craft immersive storytelling experiences, drawing upon an ‘analogue’ mindset. While immersive experiences are often associated with XR technologies, true immersion transcends the medium: it involves fostering a profound sense of engagement, presence and embodiment that shifts the user's perspective. In this context, theatre, with its empathetic and deconstructive nature, provides valuable insights by fostering emotionally rich, analogue experiences that deepen students' understanding of immersive storytelling. This study presented an educational experiment conducted within a communication design seminar, where students participated in a blended theatrical storytelling exercise. By fully immersing themselves in this experience, they unlocked their imagination and developed a deeper understanding of how emotional and sensory involvement can elevate storytelling design, regardless of the use of advanced technologies. Acting as audience members allowed future communication designers to grasp the engaging potential of t

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Visual Arts, Insecurity and an Elusive Peace in Casamance, Senegal
abstract: Abstract The separatist rebellion in Casamance, southern Senegal, has driven what is arguably the longest‐running intra‐state conflict in West Africa. Spanning over four decades, it has affected successive generations through insecurity (including armed violence and landmine use); economic disruption; trauma; human displacement (both internal and into neighbouring Guinea‐Bissau and The Gambia); loss of homes, schools and infrastructure; and through return and reconstruction processes. The paper briefly describes these impacts, particularly in the complex, dynamic security environment along Casamance's southern border with Guinea‐Bissau. It then offers three contrasting vignettes on how visual arts have been used by different actors for various ends amid an unresolved conflict, and how local people engage with these media. First, it explores how landmine awareness boards aimed at children are locally perceived. Second, it examines cultural messaging through art at a political office of the rebel movement. And third, it considers a piece of public art as an example of deploying culture for peace. The paper concludes that in promoting security and in the elusive search for a definitiv

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Critically Assessing Arts‐Based Research: Moving Forward With Tension and Care
abstract: Abstract This article is premised on the understanding that arts‐based research (ABR) has a twofold relationship with peace: the future of ABR is dependent upon conditions of scholarly peace (constructive critique and ethical practice)—a dependency that holds implications for ABR itself to serve wider movements towards peace (socially, ecologically and politically). This article presents a critical analysis of a specific mode of ABR aligned with the onto‐epistemological orientations of post‐qualitative inquiry. We contend that the anti‐methodological stance of this ABR has inadvertently fostered informal conventions and shielded ABR from constructive critique. Through an analysis of five UK‐based ABR examples, we identify three informal conventions—troublemaking, playmaking and jargon‐making—and argue that their focus neglects aesthetic quality, compromises research integrity and raises ethical concerns. In response, we offer an evaluation framework for ABR to emphasise the importance of (i) aesthetic quality, (ii) research integrity and (iii) ethical responsibility. Our critique is positioned not as an act of hostility, but as a necessary agitation, aimed at pushing ABR to more ef

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Aesthetic Dissensus as Public Pedagogy: Exploring Contemporary Art that Counters Whiteness and Far‐Right Ideologies in Mainstream Digital Spaces
abstract: Abstract Far‐right politics has re‐emerged as a significant force in mainstream Western liberal democracies, such as the United Kingdom and the United States, where it has been linked to rising levels of racial discrimination and violence that threaten to erode the fragile ideals of democratic peace within these contexts. In a 'post‐truth' era, digital aesthetics that blur the line between extremist propaganda and innocuous entertainment are being used to mainstream far‐right ideologies, including Whiteness and White racial supremacy, through sites of public pedagogy, particularly social media platforms, where they are normalised as ‘commonsense’. In response, progressive scholars have called for the mainstreaming of peaceful civic dissent in Western liberal democracies to counter the far‐right. Yet this call unfolds in a context in which democratic governments frame peaceful civic dissent—such as protests against racialised inequalities—as threats to democratic peace, rather than acts that defend democracy. As physical dissent faces heightened surveillance, digital platforms offer alternative, albeit contested, spaces for political action. However, there is a dearth of research on

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Moments of Doubts
abstract: Abstract Was it okay to bring the students here? Was it okay to plan to go here again with students working on site‐related art projects? How can art matter here? Such questions I asked myself when organizing a bachelor course on site related art in Lesvos back in 2018 and 2019. The Greek Island was then still heavily affected by the refugee crisis that hit Europe in 2015. In the visual essay I expose the uncertainty and doubt that haunted me before, throughout and after establishing and realizing the course. I focus on incidents from my experiences from Lesvos represented by images and reflections of these. All the events touch upon the ethical dilemmas that both many of the participating artists and I faced. This and other projects have made me call for a pedagogy of dissensus. When dissensus is inspiring education norms and regular ways of teaching are challenged, and possible disruptions of the expected are offered.

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Imagining—and (Re)Imaging—Peace Through Art Education

journal_name: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ART & DESIGN EDUCATION
title: Bilingual Arts Practice, Frameworks and Possibilities
abstract: Abstract This paper draws together visual arts education and the Irish language reflecting on how they have developed and evolved in the Irish primary school context. Visual arts education and the Irish language have a complex history influenced by the shifting priorities of the Irish education system. This paper explores the residual effects and challenges because of this. This work focuses on bringing together two teacher educators to explore art making through the medium of Irish and English. The collaborators explore the potential of using European frameworks to extend their practice in creating bilingual dialogue space. In doing so this bilingual arts practice between two teacher educators can be seen as a peaceful coexistence, involving translation, negotiation of meaning and oral dialogue where the act of engaging and coming in and out of both languages was ever present in the art making. This work is framed within a collaborative auto ethnographic approach. This paper represents the initial project development stage of an ongoing collaboration.
